extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students of analytic/solid geometry (classical/19th-century style)
extracted.subtask_description: Determine and classify plane sections (conics, circular sections) of second-degree surfaces and related analytic geometry constructions (chord of contact, common tangents), using algebraic criteria derived from coefficients and directional cosines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section type via AC − B^2 (criterion (8))
rubrics_metrics.description: For the quadratic equation of the planar section written A x^2 + 2B x y + C y^2 + ... , the sign of AC − B^2 (expression reduced to formula (8)) determines the species of the conic: positive → ellipse, negative → hyperbola, zero → parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The coefficients A, B, C arise after substituting the plane's directional cosines into the surface equation (see substitutions (3),(4) and formation of (6)). The reduction to (8) uses Lagrange's formulas. Apply this test to decide whether a plane cutting a second-degree surface produces an ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsoid sections: all ellipses
rubrics_metrics.description: When the surface is an ellipsoid (central surface with P, P1, P2 all positive), expression (8) is always positive and never zero; hence every plane section is an ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check signs of the principal coefficients P, P1, P2 in the surface equation aligned with principal axes: all positive ⇒ AC − B^2>0 for every plane normal (l,m,n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperboloids and cone: all section types possible
rubrics_metrics.description: For the two hyperboloids and the cone one or two of the principal coefficients (P, P1, P2) are negative; consequently the terms in (8) can combine so that (8) may be positive, negative, or zero. Thus these surfaces may be cut by planes into ellipses, hyperbolas, or parabolas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine signs of P,P1,P2: presence of negative coefficient(s) means (8) is not sign-definite; evaluate (8) for the given plane normal to classify the section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraboloids and cylinders with one zero coefficient
rubrics_metrics.description: When exactly one of the principal coefficients P, P1, P2 is zero (e.g., P2 = 0), every section by a plane parallel to the corresponding axis is a parabola; other plane sections depend on the signs of the two nonzero coefficients — they may be ellipses or hyperbolas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one coefficient is zero, substitute into the reduced form (noted as (8') in the text) and evaluate the sign. Special cases: elliptic paraboloid and elliptic cylinder → non-axial sections are ellipses; hyperbolic paraboloid and hyperbolic cylinder → non-axial sections are hyperbolas. If one of the remaining coefficients vanishes the reduced expression may be zero producing parabolic sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic cylinder: two zero coefficients ⇒ parabolas or parallel lines
rubrics_metrics.description: When two of the coefficients P, P1, P2 are zero (parabolic cylinder), the determinant/criterion (7) (i.e. equivalent of (8)) always vanishes; plane sections are all parabolas or a system of two parallel straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that exactly two principal quadratic coefficients are zero; then any plane section will be parabolic in general, with the degenerate possibility of two parallel lines (regarded as parabola of infinite radius).

rubrics_metrics.name: General-form criterion (expression (10))
rubrics_metrics.description: For a surface given under the general second-degree form, the species of the section made by any plane with direction cosines m,n, etc., is determined by the larger expression (10): the section is an ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola according as (10) is positive, negative, or zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the multilinear expression (10) (built from the general-form coefficients A_i, B_i and the plane-direction factors m,n, ...). Its sign-classifies the conic; this is the general analogue of the AC − B^2 test when axes are not necessarily principal or orthogonal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-normalized plane normals (L,M,N substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the equation of the cutting plane is given as L x + M y + N z = P with L,M,N proportional (but not normalized) to the directional cosines l,m,n, then L,M,N may be used in place of l,m,n in the criteria (8) and (10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because l,m,n are proportional to L,M,N, one may substitute the plane-coefficients directly into the determinant expressions; normalization to unit length is unnecessary when only proportionality is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for circular sections (equal coefficients and zero cross-term)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plane section is circular (in appropriately transformed coordinates) when, after aligning axes so the plane is parallel to a coordinate plane, the coefficients of y'^2 and z'^2 are equal and the coefficient of y'z' is zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform a coordinate transformation bringing the section plane parallel to e.g. the yz-plane (see use of directing cosines and elimination (11–13)). Solve the resulting simultaneous equations (11–13) (and derived relations (14)–(17)) to find planes for which the transverse quadratic coefficients are equal and the cross-term vanishes; these planes give circular sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and families of circular sections (equations (21), (22))
rubrics_metrics.description: In general there are two series of planes (given by equations (21) and (22)) producing circular sections; these series coincide for a surface of revolution and become indeterminate for a sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two series are defined by algebraic relations among the principal quadratic coefficients (Pi − Pj combinations) and the normal-direction cosines. Circular sections exist only when the relevant principal coefficients (P, P1, P2) are nonzero; if some vanish the 'circular' sections degenerate into straight lines (infinite radius). Check (21),(22) to locate the planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular-section degeneracy when principal coefficients vanish
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular sections do not exist unless the relevant principal coefficients (P, P1, P2) are nonzero; if some coefficient equals zero the corresponding quadratic coefficients in the transformed equation vanish and the 'sections' in that family reduce to straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this test to hyperbolic paraboloids and hyperbolic/parabolic cylinders (which have a zero among P, P1, P2) — they admit no true circular sections but rather rectilinear sections (degenerate circles of infinite radius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statical-moments theorem for equilibrium of three forces in a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If three forces in the same plane are in equilibrium and from any point in that plane perpendiculars are drawn to the directions of the three forces, then the rectangle contained by the resultant and its perpendicular equals the sum or difference of the rectangles contained by the component forces and their respective perpendiculars, according as the point is outside or within the angle formed by the component directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relation links resultant magnitude × its perpendicular to algebraic sums/differences of component magnitudes × their perpendiculars; use sign convention depending on the point's position relative to the angle of the component directions. The theorem refines incomplete statements appearing in some works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chord-of-contact locus for tangents to a conic from a given point
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a conic ay^ + 2b xy + c x^2 + 2d y + 2e x + f = 0 and a point (α,β), the locus of points of contact of tangents from (α,β) is given by equation (3) (constructed from combining the conic and tangent equations); for a circle this locus is itself a circle whose centre is the midpoint of the line joining the given point and the circle's centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form the tangent equation at a generic point, enforce passage through (α,β) to obtain the combined locus (3). For circles the resulting locus is explicit and geometrically interpretable: centre at midpoint between given point and original circle centre. For ellipses/hyperbolas the locus is a similar conic passing through the given point and the original centre, with its centre at the midpoint between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of points of contact for ellipse/hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ellipse (and similarly for a hyperbola), the points of contact of the two tangents drawn from a given point lie on a similar ellipse which passes through the given point and the centre of the given ellipse; the centre of this contact-ellipse is the midpoint of the line joining the given point and the original ellipse centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain by translating origin to midpoint and reducing; the constructed conic (from formula (3) specialized) yields the stated geometric relationship useful for tangent constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation and multiplicity of common tangents to two circles (four possible tangents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic elimination for the common tangent to two circles leads to up to four solutions (four common tangents in general). Depending on relative positions there are cases: intersecting circles → two real common tangents; one circle inside the other → no real common tangents; externally tangent circles → two real tangents (with two coalescing at point of contact); internally tangent → one real tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up tangent equations for each circle, equate up to constant factor, eliminate contact-point coordinates to obtain quartic-like condition (see (23) and subsequent reductions). Analyze discriminants/R expressions to decide number and reality of tangents. Special symmetric reductions yield geometric interpretations: some tangent intersection lines coincide with line joining centres or are perpendicular to it (see equations (24),(25),(26)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality/imaginarity criteria for imaginary exponentials (classification of (−k)^a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifications for when expressions like (−k)^a (and related complex-exponential forms) are real or imaginary: (1) if k>0 and a is any real → expression real; (2) if k<0 and a integer or rational with odd denominator → expression real; (3) if k<0 and a has even denominator → expression imaginary; (4) if k<0 and a is not a finite number (e.g., results from infinite-series-generating operations) the expression may be sometimes real or sometimes imaginary depending on detailed expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules follow from expansion and parity of fractional exponents; when dealing with complex bases or multi-valued fractional exponents examine the generating functions and branch choices. The text presents propositions (I–VII) developing these criteria and examples (Euler's constant e representation) showing typical behavior.
